states.summary: AI-generated intimate-image rules, plus consumer-protection and breach-notification duties relevant to AI products and data use. Each has its own scope and exceptions.

laws.title: Unfair and deceptive trade practices
laws.description: General unfair-trade rules can apply to misleading AI product claims, sales practices and services. They are not an AI-specific approval or certification regime.
laws.appliesTo: Business activities in or affecting commerce; the statute expressly excludes professional services rendered by members of a learned profession.
obligations: Do not use unfair or deceptive practices in covered commerce.
laws.enforcement: An injured person may sue under §75-16; assessed damages are trebled.
laws.limits: The professional-services exclusion is activity-specific; do not assume every business associated with a professional is exempt. The advertising-media exception also has conditions.
practicalSteps: Keep evidence supporting claims about AI accuracy, safety and capabilities.
Review sales copy and chatbot statements before publication.

laws.title: Personal information: breach notification
laws.description: AI-related data exposure can trigger existing breach-notification duties when the statutory personal-information and breach definitions are met.
laws.timing: Existing law; notification deadlines run from discovery or notification.
laws.appliesTo: Covered businesses owning/licensing personal information, and custodians maintaining others’ data.
obligations: Notify affected people without unreasonable delay, subject to permitted investigative and law-enforcement delays.
A custodian must notify the owner/licensee immediately after discovery.
Notify the Attorney General when consumer notice is given; more than 1,000 notices also trigger nationwide credit-reporting-agency notice.
laws.enforcement: Violation is treated as a §75-1.1 violation; an individual must suffer resulting injury to bring a private claim.
laws.limits: Not every prompt leak meets the definitions. Apply §75-61 and the special exclusions in §75-65(a); notice timing is not a fixed 30-day rule.

codeSections.detail: Definitions of protected information and security breach

practicalSteps: Identify data owners and escalation contacts before using an external AI vendor.
Keep an incident plan that separates owner, custodian and regulator notices.

laws.title: AI-generated intimate images: disclosure restrictions
laws.description: The private-image law expressly includes realistic depictions generated or modified using algorithms or AI.
laws.timing: Existing statute; AI-image language appears in the 2024 amendment.
laws.appliesTo: Knowingly disclosing identifiable intimate imagery with specified harmful intent, without affirmative consent, and with the required creation/privacy circumstances.
obligations: Do not disclose covered imagery where all §14-190.5A(b) elements are met.
laws.enforcement: Criminal penalties apply; affected people also have a civil action, including statutory damages and possible image-destruction relief.
laws.limits: Not a ban on all synthetic images. Statutory exceptions include specified public-interest uses and service providers hosting another person’s images. The civil filing period is limited.
practicalSteps: Do not treat an AI label as permission to publish intimate depictions.
Create a reporting and escalation route for suspected nonconsensual imagery.

states.summary: Synthetic intimate-image restrictions, breach-notification requirements and consumer-protection rules relevant to AI publishing, products and data handling.

laws.title: Nonconsensual intimate images, including digital forgeries
laws.description: The law covers realistic digitally forged intimate images, including machine-generated depictions. A label saying an image is artificial does not remove it from the definition.
laws.appliesTo: Intentional dissemination without effective consent, with the statutory knowledge/privacy conditions.
obligations: Do not disseminate covered intimate imagery without effective consent. Consent to creation or private sharing is not automatically consent to further dissemination.
laws.enforcement: Graduated criminal penalties apply; harmful intent or financial gain can trigger felony treatment.
laws.limits: Read the knowledge and reasonable-expectation-of-privacy elements and law-enforcement exception. The statute is specific to intimate imagery, not every AI replica.

codeSections.detail: Digital forgery, identity and effective-consent definitions

practicalSteps: Check permission for dissemination separately from permission to create an image.
Escalate suspected intimate-image abuse promptly.

laws.title: Personal identifying information: breach notification
laws.description: Existing notification rules can apply when AI systems or vendors expose covered identifying data.
laws.timing: Existing law; notices are due without unreasonable delay.
laws.appliesTo: Businesses operating in South Carolina that own/license covered data; separate duties apply to custodians.
obligations: Notify affected residents when the breach meets the illegal-use/material-risk-of-harm test.
Custodians must notify the owner/licensee immediately after discovery.
If notifying more than 1,000 people at once, notify Consumer Affairs and nationwide consumer reporting agencies.
laws.enforcement: Injured residents have specified civil remedies. Knowing and wilful violations can attract Consumer Affairs fines.
laws.limits: Encryption/redaction, data definitions, law-enforcement delays and qualifying financial-institution exceptions matter.
practicalSteps: Map whether your organization owns or only processes the exposed data.
Record the harm assessment and notice decision.

laws.title: Unfair Trade Practices Act and AI marketing
laws.description: Unfair or deceptive AI sales claims and commercial practices can engage the state’s general trade-practices law.
laws.appliesTo: Trade and commerce affecting South Carolina, subject to statutory exclusions and applicable legal standards.
obligations: Do not use unfair or deceptive methods in covered trade or commerce.
laws.enforcement: The Attorney General can seek relief and civil penalties. Section 39-5-140 permits qualifying individual damages claims; wilful/knowing violations can yield treble damages.
laws.limits: Section 39-5-40 exempts specified permitted transactions and certain advertising intermediaries. A dispute or inaccurate output alone does not establish every element of a claim.
practicalSteps: Check evidence behind model-performance and professional-service claims.
Retain advertised promises and relevant customer communications.

states.summary: Consumer claims, SSN handling and customer-record disposal: general statutory duties that can matter when using or selling AI. These entries are not a comprehensive survey of Georgia AI legislation.

laws.title: Fair Business Practices Act and AI representations
laws.description: General consumer-protection rules apply to unfair or deceptive commercial representations, including claims made about an AI service.
laws.timing: Existing law. Current Attorney General explanation checked; linked code compilation is labeled 2021.
laws.appliesTo: Consumer transactions principally for personal, family or household purposes, with separate statutory scope and exceptions.
obligations: Avoid unfair or deceptive consumer acts and practices.
laws.enforcement: The Attorney General enforces the Act in the public interest. Qualifying private claims under §10-1-399 generally require a written demand at least 30 days before filing.
laws.limits: Not a general regulation of every business-to-business AI transaction. Check the current code before relying on remedies or filing deadlines.
practicalSteps: Substantiate AI capability claims and make limitations clear.
Keep screenshots, contracts and sales communications if challenging a misleading service.

sources.label: Attorney General · Act scope and enforcement

laws.title: Social Security numbers in AI workflows
laws.description: Specific SSN safeguards matter when AI tools handle intake forms, identifiers or generated reports.
laws.timing: Existing statute. Official explanatory material checked; linked AG compilation is labeled 2021.
laws.appliesTo: Persons, firms and corporations handling SSNs, subject to enumerated exceptions.
obligations: Do not publicly display SSNs.
Do not require online transmission without a secure connection or encryption, or use an SSN alone as website authentication.
laws.enforcement: The provision sits within the Fair Business Practices Act; applicable remedies depend on the facts and statutory requirements.
laws.limits: Exceptions include legally required uses and specified internal administrative uses. These rules do not authorize otherwise unlawful data sharing.

codeSections.detail: Public display, transmission and authentication rules

practicalSteps: Redact SSNs from prompts, demos and generated public documents.
Check intake security and access controls.

sources.label: University System of Georgia · statutory overview

laws.title: Safe disposal of customer records
laws.description: Existing disposal rules are relevant to customer records used in AI workflows, including records containing identifiers, medical information or account details.
laws.timing: Existing statutory requirement; Attorney General explanation checked.
laws.appliesTo: Businesses discarding customer records containing protected personal information.
obligations: Use shredding, erasure, unreadable modification or another qualifying safeguard against unauthorized access when disposing of protected records.
laws.enforcement: The Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Division provides the linked compliance information and complaint route.
laws.limits: The disposal requirement does not itself set a universal retention period. Names, addresses and telephone numbers alone receive different treatment; preservation duties may require retaining records.

codeSections.detail: Disposal safeguards explained by the Attorney General

practicalSteps: Include AI input files, exported transcripts and vendor copies in the records-disposal process.
Confirm what the vendor actually deletes when an account or file is removed.

states.summary: Political AI disclosures, consumer profiling rights, sensitive-data sales, data security and recording consent. Scope differs sharply across these statutes; the main privacy-law revenue threshold is not a general exemption from Florida law.

laws.title: Generative AI in political advertising
laws.description: Specified political communications using generative AI to depict a real person doing something that did not occur require an AI disclaimer.
laws.appliesTo: Covered political advertisements and electioneering communications with intent to injure a candidate or deceive about a ballot issue.
obligations: Include the statutory AI disclaimer in addition to other election disclaimers.
Meet format rules: print minimum 12-point bold; video visible throughout at least 4% of picture height; audio at least 3 seconds. Internet/graphic requirements also apply.
laws.enforcement: The Florida Elections Commission accepts complaints; failure to disclose can carry civil and criminal penalties.
laws.limits: Not a labeling mandate for every use of AI in political work; the depiction and intent conditions must be met.
practicalSteps: Review the exact disclaimer text in the statute before releasing creative.
Check every format and channel, including audio and mobile graphics.

laws.title: Digital Bill of Rights: profiling, sensitive data and consumer requests
laws.description: The main privacy framework is narrowly scoped, but includes profiling opt-outs relevant to AI. A separate sensitive-data-sale rule has broader business coverage.
laws.appliesTo: Main controllers generally need more than $1 billion in global annual gross revenue plus a qualifying online-advertising, smart-speaker/virtual-assistant or large app-store business model; controlled/controlling entities also matter. Section 501.715 separately reaches qualifying for-profit Florida businesses collecting consumer data without the billion-dollar threshold.
obligations: Covered controllers must honor statutory access, correction, deletion, portability and opt-out rights, including significant-decision profiling.
Provide accessible request channels under §501.709.
Check §501.715 before selling sensitive data: prior consent and a prescribed website notice may be required even outside the main controller threshold.
laws.enforcement: Department of Legal Affairs enforcement; up to $50,000 per violation, with specified enhancements. The law creates no private action.
laws.limits: Consumers exclude employment and commercial contexts. Section 501.703 contains significant entity/data exemptions. Small size alone does not resolve §501.715.
practicalSteps: Document the threshold and exemption analysis before assuming the law does not apply.
Trace profiling, biometric and sensitive-data uses separately.

laws.title: Data security and breach reporting
laws.description: AI vendors and users handling covered personal information can face security and breach duties without the Digital Bill of Rights’ revenue threshold.
laws.timing: Existing law; the current 2026 code includes security, notification and disposal duties.
laws.appliesTo: Commercial covered entities and contracted processors; governmental entities have specified duties.
obligations: Use reasonable security measures and secure disposal.
Affected-person notice is generally due within 30 days after determining or having reason to believe a breach occurred.
Notify Legal Affairs within 30 days for 500 or more affected Florida individuals; processors generally notify their customer within 10 days.
laws.enforcement: Department of Legal Affairs enforcement; no private cause of action under this section.
laws.limits: Protected data includes specified identifiers, medical information, biometric data, geolocation and account credentials. Statutory exceptions, documented no-harm determinations and permitted delays require separate assessment.
practicalSteps: Assign incident ownership before sending personal information to an AI provider.
Require rapid vendor incident escalation and track the applicable notice clocks.

laws.title: AI meeting assistants and recording consent
laws.description: AI recording and transcription must fit Florida’s existing interception law. For ordinary consensual recording of covered communications, the statute requires prior consent from all parties.
laws.appliesTo: People intercepting covered wire, oral or electronic communications. Oral-communication coverage depends on a justified expectation against interception.
obligations: Obtain all-party prior consent when relying on §934.03(2)(d).
Do not unlawfully intercept, use or disclose covered communications.
laws.enforcement: Section 934.03 provides criminal penalties; additional remedies may apply under Chapter 934.
laws.limits: There are specific statutory exceptions. This is not a universal rule that every public conversation is protected, nor does Florida consent settle other jurisdictions or confidentiality duties.
practicalSteps: Confirm participant locations and consent before enabling an AI notetaker.
Offer a meeting option without recording and review transcript access and retention.
